title: Rebecca: The Rose of Jerusalem and the Secret of the Tent of Miracles
source_file: השושנה המאירה_ סיפורה של רבקה אמנו.docx
content:
Rebecca: The Rose of Jerusalem and the Secret of the Tent of Miracles
Hello to you, dear and sweet children. Sit with me for a moment, close your eyes and imagine a very faraway land, a place where the sand is golden and the sun is always smiling. Today I want to tell you about a wonderful personality, a mother of us all, who lived in a world of thorns but managed to be the most beautiful flower in God's garden. This girl was called Rebecca. Our story is not only about what once was, but about the light that exists inside each one of you. It is a story about a well of water that became a test of love, about a magical journey within clouds of glory, and about one deep secret hidden inside old clothes. Ready? Let's set out.
1. Chapter One: The White Rose in the Field of Thorns
In the heart of the city of Haran, in a large and splendid house, little Rebecca grew up. But this house was not an ordinary one. Her father, Bethuel, and her brother, Laban, were known throughout the region as "men of deceit." They were champions at saying one thing and doing another. They thought only about themselves, about money and about honor. All around them, the people were prickly and unpleasant, just like thorns in a field. But Rebecca? She was a wonder. Our Sages called her "a rose among the thorns." Imagine a white, delicate rose with a sweet scent, growing right in the middle of a thicket of gray, sharp thorns. The thorns try to prick it, but it stays soft. The thorns try to hide the sun, but it always turns toward the light. Rebecca did not learn from the lies of her brother Laban. She chose a completely different path. Here are three qualities that shone in the soul of little Rebecca, qualities that made her "the architect of the nation":
Nobility of truth: In a world where everyone cheated, Rebecca was careful about every word. Her speech was as clear as pure water. She understood that truth is the foundation of everything holy.
A good and compassionate eye: While those around her looked for ways to profit at the expense of others, Rebecca always looked for the good. She saw a sad person, and at once she wanted to make him happy. She saw an injured animal, and at once she wanted to help.
Courage of the heart: Although she was very young (the Midrash tells that she was only fourteen years old when she set out on her way), she had the inner strength of a giant. She was not afraid to be different. She knew that she belonged to the world of kindness. Far away from there, in the land of Canaan, sat Abraham our Patriarch. He was looking for a bride for his beloved son Isaac. Abraham was not looking for riches or palaces. He was looking for this "rose." He knew that only a girl who had grown up among the "thorns" and remained pure could be the mother who would build the people of Israel and teach us how to turn darkness into light. Transition sentence: The sun began to paint the skies of Haran in shades of orange and purple, and Rebecca went out, as was her custom, to the well, not knowing that a small act of kindness was about to change the face of history.
2. Chapter Two: The Secret of the Well of Water and the Thirsty Camels
Beside the ancient well stood a stranger. It was Eliezer, Abraham's servant. He was tired from the journey, and his clothes were covered with the dust of the desert. Beside him stood ten large camels, kneeling under their loads, their tongues hanging out with thirst. Eliezer prayed to God to send him a sign. He wanted to see "altruism" – a rather hard word, isn't it? It means doing good simply because it is good, without thinking at all, "What will I get out of it?" Eliezer turned to Rebecca and asked in a hoarse voice: "Let me sip, I pray you, a little water from your pitcher." He asked for only a small sip, a mouthful to quench his thirst. Rebecca did not just say "yes." She acted with amazing speed. "Drink, my lord," she said with a smile, and at once lowered the heavy pitcher from her shoulder. But then she saw the camels. She knew that a camel that is thirsty after a long journey needs lots and lots of water. She did not wait for anyone to ask her. Let us see in a table how great her generosity was:| What Eliezer asked for | What Rebecca did (in pure kindness) || ------ | ------ || "A little water" – a small sip just for him. | She drew water again and again for Eliezer and his servants until they had drunk their fill. || Nothing for the animals – he did not want to burden her. | She said: "I will draw for your camels also, until they have finished drinking." || Rest – he expected her to go home. | She ran back and forth to the deep well, again and again, for ten camels! |
Eliezer stood there "gazing at her." He kept silent. He wanted to see whether she would grow tired, whether she would ask for money, or perhaps stop in the middle and say "This is too hard." But Rebecca kept going. Every bucket of water she brought up from the well was full of love. Eliezer understood that she was not doing it for a gift, but because her heart simply could not see a thirsty creature without helping. Her "camels" (gemalim) became "acts of loving-kindness" (gemilut chesed). Transition sentence: When Rebecca agreed to set out on the journey, she did not know that the road itself was about to become a carpet of light beneath the feet of her camels.
3. Chapter Three: The Shining Journey and Deborah the Good Companion
The journey from Haran to Canaan should have taken many days, but God wanted to bring the rose to her garden quickly. The Midrash tells that the road "leaped" toward them. The skies were not ordinary; flashes and sparks of divine light lit up the night, and the whole road seemed lit with a wondrous light, as though the angels were accompanying the caravan 1, 3. Beside Rebecca rode an older woman with a kind face and wise eyes. This was Deborah the nurse. Deborah was not just a nanny; she was a "spiritual grandmother." Every night, under the light of the stars, Deborah would whisper to Rebecca stories about Sarah our Matriarch, about the tent that was wide open on every side and about the holiness awaiting her in the Land of Israel. She helped Rebecca prepare her soul, raising it higher and higher in the levels of holiness so that she would be worthy of Isaac the righteous 2. A point to think about: Deborah the nurse was so devoted that she remained part of the family forever. Many years later, when Jacob (Rebecca's son) needed help to return home from exile, Rebecca sent none other than Deborah to strengthen him. Deborah teaches us that whoever invests in children with love and good education becomes part of the family's heart for generations 2. Transition sentence: Suddenly, on the horizon, there appeared the figure of a man walking in the field at sunset. The light of the road met the special light of Isaac.
4. Chapter Four: The Shining Tent and the Three Miracles That Returned
When Rebecca saw Isaac from afar, she felt something powerful that she had never felt before. Isaac was standing in the field in the afternoon prayer (Mincha), and his face shone with a sublime light. He looked to her like an angel of God, awesome and majestic, a spiritual figure who was wholly "a perfect burnt offering" 4, 17. Out of great reverence and a good kind of shame, Rebecca almost fell from the camel and hurried to cover herself with a veil. She understood that she was entering a world of deep holiness. Isaac brought Rebecca into the tent of his mother, Sarah our Matriarch. Ever since Sarah had died, the tent had been dark and sad. But the moment Rebecca set foot inside, the light returned! Our Sages tell of three wondrous miracles that shone again thanks to Rebecca:
The burning candle: Rebecca lit a candle on Sabbath eve, and wonder of wonders, the candle did not go out! It went on burning with a soft, bright light throughout the whole week, day and night, until the next Sabbath eve. This was a sign that Rebecca's soul is always connected to the light of God 11.
The blessing in the dough: When Rebecca kneaded the dough to make challot, a special blessing came upon it. A little dough was enough to satisfy many guests, and the bread tasted of the Garden of Eden. This showed that every material thing that Rebecca touches becomes holy 11.
The cloud tied to the tent: Above Rebecca's tent there always rested a soft white cloud, the cloud of the Divine Presence (Shekhinah). This cloud protected the home and guarded it from all harm, a sign that God dwelt inside their home permanently 11. Rebecca made the tent the most radiant place in the world. She proved that a righteous woman can turn walls of cloth into a dwelling place of the Divine Presence. Transition sentence: The years went by, and inside this shining tent Rebecca understood that she had another fateful task – to guard the pure spark that would carry on the people of Israel.
5. Chapter Five: The Special Garments and the Great Promise
Two sons were born to Rebecca, Jacob and Esau. Jacob was a plain man, dwelling in tents, and Esau was a man of the field. Rebecca, in her prophetic wisdom, saw what others did not see. She understood that "the garment does not decide." When Isaac wanted to bless his sons, Rebecca knew that the blessings had to reach Jacob. She had Jacob put on Esau's "goodly garments." Why? Because she wanted to teach us a deep secret: sometimes there are Jews who outwardly look like "Esau," dressed in everyday clothes and seemingly far from the Torah. But Rebecca knew that inside every such person there is a "spark of holiness." When Isaac smelled Jacob's clothes, he did not smell the scent of an ordinary field. The Midrash says that he smelled the "scent of his traitors" (bogdav, read in place of begadav, "his garments") – even those who feel far away (traitors) carry the scent of the Garden of Eden when they do a good deed 21, 22. Rebecca taught us that we must love every Jew, because beneath the outer "garment" there is always a shining soul. Rebecca made Jacob a promise that makes the heart tremble to this day. She said to him: "Now, my son, hearken (shema)." She saw through the holy spirit that one day all of Jacob's children – the whole people of Israel – would stand together and be completely righteous. She saw us, the children of today, standing in the morning and in the evening and saying: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One." She promised that "his bed is complete" – that each one of us is an inseparable part of the holy chain 1.
Conclusion: The Rose That Stays with Us
Dear children, the story of Rebecca our Matriarch did not end in that tent thousands of years ago. Every time you give way to a friend, every time you say a word of truth, and every time you girls light Sabbath candles – you become Rebecca's rose. Rebecca teaches us that no matter where we are, even if all around us there are thorns of falsehood or anger, we can stay white, pure and full of kindness. Rebecca's light, the blessing in the dough and the guarding cloud are in the heart of each one of you. Always remember the promise of Mother Rebecca: you are her children, and your light will never go out.

title: The Work, Torah Teaching and Leadership Standing of Rebecca Our Matriarch: An Exegetical, Theological and Educational Analysis
source_file: פועלה, משנתה התורנית ומעמדה המנהיגותי של רבקה אמנו_ ניתוח פרשני, תיאולוגי וחינוכי.docx
content:
The Work, Torah Teaching and Leadership Standing of Rebecca Our Matriarch: An Exegetical, Theological and Educational Analysis
This article sets out an in-depth, multidimensional analysis of the figure of Rebecca our Matriarch, emphasizing her spiritual independence and her ability to grow as "a rose among the thorns" in the midst of a morally corrupt environment. The text examines her leadership role through central junctures in her life, from the prophetic initiative she took during her difficult pregnancy to the strategic maneuver in the episode of the blessings, which was intended to ensure the continuity of the line through Jacob. The source offers a critical and educational look at the failures in the home of Isaac, drawing on a wide range of classical and modern commentaries that illuminate Rebecca's theological motives. The aim of the work is to present Rebecca as the architect of the nation's future, whose daring actions sanctified the inner essence of the people of Israel beyond its outer shell.
The Work, Torah Teaching and Leadership Standing of Rebecca Our Matriarch: An Exegetical, Theological and Educational Analysis
A Rose among the Thorns: The Background in the House of Bethuel and the Growth of a Woman of Kindness
The spiritual and moral growth of Rebecca our Matriarch is one of the most wondrous phenomena in the history of the Patriarchs and Matriarchs. She grew up in Haran, in the house of Bethuel the Aramean and in the surroundings of her brother Laban – an environment marked by ingrained deceit, greed for money and idolatry.[1, 2] The Sages defined this reality with the image of "a rose among the thorns," which expresses her ability to preserve her moral purity and her spiritual immunity without being harmed or pricked by the negative influences of her surroundings.[2] This sharp contrast between Rebecca and her surroundings is heightened in the light of the midrash describing the reception that her father, Bethuel, held for Eliezer, Abraham's servant.[1, 3] Bethuel, who coveted the guest's great wealth, tried to poison Eliezer by serving him a bowl of stew containing a deadly poison.[1, 3] The midrash tells that the angel Gabriel switched the bowls, and so Bethuel met his own death from the poison that he himself had prepared.[1, 3]
In complete contrast to this toxic and greedy atmosphere, Rebecca is revealed at the well as a symbol of active kindness, vitality and exceptional alacrity in performing commandments.[4, 5] Her description in Scripture as "a virgin, and no man had known her" receives a profound midrashic interpretation: the doubled wording teaches that not only was she a virgin, but that no man – including the servant Eliezer, who is called "the man" in the verses – violated her privacy or touched her during the journey.[4] She remained entirely protected and pure from any foreign contact.[4] Her quality of kindness is not merely a private character trait but an existential foundation for the building of the nation, as emphasized in Midrash Tanchuma, which states that the whole Torah – its beginning, its middle and its end – is based on acts of loving-kindness.[2] Symbolically, the death of Deborah, Rebecca's nurse and educator, is defined as the "middle" of a Torah characterized by kindness.[2]
Deborah the nurse, called in Targum Yonatan "padagogta" (her educator), served as a decisive mediating factor in Rebecca's growth.[2] Deborah was apparently one of the souls whom Abraham and Sarah had drawn near in Haran, and it was she who implanted in Rebecca the values of monotheism and of the ethics of Abraham's house, despite the influences of her corrupt family.[2] This bond was so deep that Deborah accompanied Rebecca on her journey to Canaan in order to continue guiding her in holiness [2], and later she was even sent by Rebecca to Haran to bring Jacob our Patriarch back to the Land of Israel.[2]
The depth of Rebecca's personality is already hinted at in her name; the root "rbq" points to a texture of connection ("a harness of connection" or "a yoke"), which teaches about her conception of marriage as a shared and inseparable bearing of the yoke of life and of the spiritual mission.[3] Isaac our Patriarch immediately recognized in her the successor of his mother Sarah, and her inner holiness led his love for her to grow ever greater as he came to know her righteousness after their marriage.[3] This bond lasted throughout their eighty-four years of marriage, up to the days of the blessings.[6] Despite her holiness, her complex future was already hinted at when she set out on her way: the midrash on the verse "and they rode upon the camels" compares the camel, which bears signs of both impurity and purity, to Rebecca, who was destined to bring forth a righteous offspring and a wicked offspring.[4] On that same occasion the moral order of the world was also hinted at, as the midrash remarks on the words "and they followed the man" that it is unseemly for a man to walk behind a woman, and in this way the bounds of modesty and of proper conduct on the road were made clear.[4]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
"And She Went to Inquire of the Lord": The Crisis of Pregnancy and Rebecca's Theological Struggle
Rebecca's longed-for pregnancy, which came after twenty years of barrenness and of shared prayers, quickly became a source of deep physical and spiritual suffering, described in the words "and the children struggled together within her."[4, 7] The lack of clarity about what was happening in her womb brought about in Rebecca an acute crisis of faith and of existence, which led her to turn, independently and inspiringly, to the sources of prophecy.[8, 9]
The table below presents a comprehensive comparison between five central exegetical approaches that analyze the nature of the struggling, the meaning of Rebecca's cry ("Why am I thus?", lamah zeh anokhi) and the object of the divine inquiry:
An examination of the verses reveals that Rebecca's going to inquire of the Lord holds a groundbreaking dimension.[7, 8] The midrash notes that the study house of Shem and Eber was regarded as a place where the Divine Presence rests, and whoever greets an elder there is as though he greeted the Divine Presence.[7] Likewise, an opinion is cited that Shem the son of Noah himself was at times called "the Lord" because he was the foremost representative of God on earth.[8] The precise wording of Scripture, "And the Lord said to her," gives rise to an exegetical discussion: the use of the word "to her" (lah) emphasizes that God spoke to her in a unique way, whether through a messenger-prophet who mediated the answer or through direct revelation, and thereby established her standing as a prophetess and as an independent figure worthy of dialogue with God.[7]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Educational Split in the Home of Isaac and Rebecca and the Critique of Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch
As the boys grew up, the abysmal difference between them became clear: Esau became a wild man of the field, while Jacob remained in the tents of Torah as a plain man.[4] This difference created a deep fault line in their shared parenting, as Isaac tended to love Esau out of a certain conception, while Rebecca gave her love and devotion to Jacob.[4]
Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch offers a trenchant and innovative analysis of the educational failure that characterized the home of the Patriarchs in that generation.[11] According to him, the Sages never refrained from exposing the errors of the fathers of the nation in order to teach us a lesson for the generations.[11] The basic educational mistake of Isaac and Rebecca was ignoring the innate differences in the children's characters, differences that were known to them even before the birth through the prophecy.[11] Instead of educating each boy according to the unique inclinations of his soul, they were guided by a uniform and rigid method of education.[11] Had they applied the rule "Train a youth according to his way," they could have channeled Esau's vital, wild and active powers ("a man of the field") toward the service of God in his own way.[11] The attempt to fit both of them into the same spiritual mold ultimately led to Esau's complete estrangement and to his educational ruin.[11]
Classical commentary offers various explanations for the parents' preferences:
Isaac's approach (according to Radak): Isaac was well aware that Esau was not righteous and that his character traits were flawed.[12] Precisely for this reason he held that Esau needed his material and spiritual blessing in order to rise and find his way.[12] Jacob, by contrast, was a perfected righteous man and did not need these blessings, since the historic blessing of Abraham (the land and the covenant) was assured to him in any case.[12]
Esau's deception (according to Rashi): Esau deceived his father and presented himself as meticulous in the commandments by means of baseless halakhic questions, such as "How does one tithe salt and straw?"[3] Isaac, who did not see reality as it is, was influenced by the "game" in his son's mouth.[3]
Rebecca's view: Rebecca, who foresaw the future in prophecy and knew that "the elder shall serve the younger," recognized Jacob as the true and exclusive continuer of the line.[1, 6] The midrash emphasizes her exceeding righteousness and notes that she was worthy in her own right that the full continuity of the nation (the twelve tribes) should come forth from her directly, by virtue of her pure love for the spiritual truth represented by Jacob.[1]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Drama of the Blessings: A Strategic Maneuver to Preserve the Sanctity of the Line
Rebecca's decision to act by way of cunning and to dress Jacob in Esau's garments in order to win his father's blessings is one of the most dramatic junctures in Scripture.[6] This act, which took place after 84 years of marriage, was done "behind Isaac's back" and left a painful mark on the history of the family.[6] Nevertheless, a deep examination of the motives reveals a profound theological system of considerations, free of personal interests.[1, 9]
Nahmanides (Ramban) analyzes in detail the reasons why Rebecca chose the path of an indirect maneuver, instead of turning to Isaac and revealing to him the prophecy she had received during her pregnancy ("and the elder shall serve the younger") [9, 13]:
Modesty and personal ethics: Since Rebecca had gone to inquire of the Lord without taking explicit permission from Isaac, she felt embarrassment and discomfort at revealing to him after the fact the personal prophecy she had received.[9, 13]
The honor of Isaac as a prophet: Rebecca held that it was not fitting that she, who had received prophecy through a messenger, should instruct Isaac – who was a great and exalted prophet – how to act.[9, 13]
The fear of leaving matters to Heaven: Rebecca knew that Isaac loved Esau.[9] She feared that if she revealed the prophecy to him now, he would indeed refrain from blessing Esau so as not to transgress God's word, but out of pain and disappointment he would also not want to give the blessings to Jacob.[9] In such a situation, Isaac would have left the decision to the passive mercies of Heaven without giving any blessing at all.[9]
A blessing with a whole heart: Rebecca wanted Jacob to win the blessings out of his father's free will and full intention.[9] The deception allowed Isaac to give the blessings willingly and with enormous love, thinking that he was blessing his beloved son.[9]
An intended divine decree: The course of events was part of a cosmic plan intended to ensure that Jacob would win the blessing of the covenant and of the land, while Esau would receive the blessing of the sword that suited his character.[9]
To prepare Jacob for the occasion, Rebecca took significant symbolic steps.[9, 13] When she describes Isaac's words to him, she adds of her own accord the words "before the Lord" (Genesis 27:7), words that Isaac himself had not said to Esau.[9, 13] This addition was intended to make clear to Jacob that this was not an ordinary human blessing but a prophetic and spiritual occasion upon which the Divine Presence rested, and therefore there was no going back from it.[9, 13] Nahmanides (Ramban) emphasizes Rebecca's righteousness in the expression "Esau her elder son and Jacob her younger son" – although human nature tends to prefer the firstborn and to honor him, Rebecca rose above natural maternal feeling and acted out of an absolute conception of justice that preferred the righteous younger son over the wicked elder one.[9]
Hasidic thought gives an additional existential-theological layer to the fascinating choice to dress Jacob in Esau's garments.[6] According to this explanation, Rebecca did not want to remove Esau entirely from the line, but sought to create a spiritual platform that would preserve an eternal bond with all her descendants in times to come.[6] She foresaw the future and understood that throughout the history of the people of Israel there would be Jews whose outward appearance would resemble that of "Esau" – Jews who would look like "men of the field" and would take off the garments of tradition in favor of the clothes of the modern, foreign world.[6]
Had Jacob received the blessings only in his natural garments as a perfect Jew ("dwelling in tents"), the blessing would have belonged only to those who look and behave without blemish.[6] By dressing Jacob in Esau's garments, Rebecca established a revolutionary principle: the outer garment does not determine a person's essence; the Jewish soul and the spiritual genes remain eternal and unchangeable.[6] This act gives strength to every Jew in every generation to rise above his outer shell and to remember that he always remains an inseparable part of the people of Israel and of the blessing of his fathers.[6]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Consequences of the Blessing, the Existential Struggle and Historical Continuity
The discovery of the deception led to a heartrending human drama: Esau's great and bitter cry, and Isaac's realization that indeed "yea, and he shall be blessed."[12, 13] Isaac, accepting the divine decree, in the end blesses Esau as well, but this blessing is essentially different from the one Jacob received.[9, 12, 13]
The following table presents a comparative analysis of the two blessings the brothers received and their historical consequences:
Nahmanides (Ramban) interprets the words "and it shall come to pass when you are aggrieved" (ve-haya ka'asher tarid) as a prophetic warning to Israel: when Esau complains and grieves over Jacob's yoke, he will have the ability to throw it off, and therefore the children of Israel are warned not to oppress Esau or to provoke him excessively.[9]
Esau's immediate reaction was murderous planning to take revenge on Jacob, who was forced to hide from him.[9, 12] Rashi interprets the word "consoles himself" (mitnachem) in connection with Esau in two ways: he regretted the closeness of brotherhood and began to think murderous thoughts, or he had already drunk over him a "cup of consolation" and regarded Jacob as dead in his eyes.[12] Rebecca's recognition of the danger led her to cry out: "Why should I be bereaved of you both in one day?"[3, 12] While Rashbam interprets this on the practical level – that if Esau murdered Jacob, he himself would be put to death by the blood avengers [12] – Rashi cites the homily of the Sages according to which the holy spirit entered Rebecca and she prophesied an exact prophecy that her two sons would in fact die on the very same day.[12]
At this stage Rebecca is revealed as the architect of the nation's future.[2, 3] She turns to Isaac with a focused argument combining spiritual and existential concern: "I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth... what good is life to me?"[3] This step led to Jacob being sent to Haran to find a worthy partner, and thereby the assimilation of the continuer of the line was prevented.[3] Rebecca's influence continued throughout the twenty years of Jacob's exile with Laban as well.[2] When Jacob hesitated to return to the Land, it was Rebecca who sent Deborah her nurse – the educational authority of the family – to move him to leave the exile and return to the land of Canaan.[2]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary
The Torah teaching and historical work of Rebecca our Matriarch shape her figure as a spiritual and political leader with an unprecedented vision of the future. She grew as "a rose among the thorns," preserved the purity of kindness in the face of the greed of her father's house, and became the first woman in Scripture to initiate an independent prophetic and theological appeal in the face of life's crises.
While Isaac sought to act out of compassion and a desire to correct Esau by means of the blessings, Rebecca recognized with a sober prophetic and educational eye that the future of the line depended on placing Jacob at the head of the nation. Her daring decision to use cunning and to dress Jacob in Esau's garments was not an act of family conspiracy, but a deep spiritual maneuver intended to ensure that the blessing would take effect with a whole heart, to preserve the sanctity of the covenant, and to give eternal strength to every Jew throughout the generations – even one dressed in the garments of "the man of the field" – to know that his soul and his identity always remain bound to the root of the nation. The figure of Rebecca remains an eternal model of complex parenting, of leadership in a time of crisis and of standing firm on guard over the sanctity of the generations.

title: The Leadership Work and Torah Teaching of Rebecca Our Matriarch: A Philosophical, Hermeneutic and Historiographical Analysis of the Architect of the Nation

content:
The Leadership Work and Torah Teaching of Rebecca Our Matriarch: A Philosophical, Hermeneutic and Historiographical Analysis of the Architect of the Nation
The work draws the portrait of Rebecca our Matriarch as "the architect of the nation," analyzing her leadership and spiritual role as a figure who combines autonomous moral resilience with an activism of kindness. The text examines her unique ability to grow as "a rose among the thorns" in a corrupt environment, her existential struggle with the crisis of pregnancy and prophecy, and the complex relationship with Isaac, which was marked by reverence and a communication gap. The work emphasizes that Rebecca's moves, and in particular the strategy of the blessings, were not a simple act of deception but a leadership decision intended to ensure the continuity of the people of Israel and the purity of its seed for the generations. By combining the sources of the Sages, classical commentary and Hasidic thought, the work presents Rebecca as the one who laid the metaphysical foundation for the people's ability to clarify sparks of holiness even in situations of exile and concealment.

A Rose among the Thorns: Rebecca's Lineage, Birth and Spiritual Adaptation
Rebecca our Matriarch, the second female figure in the line of the Matriarchs of the people of Israel, was born in Paddan Aram, in Haran, to Bethuel the son of Nahor, and was the sister of Laban the Aramean [cite: 1]. Her family and social world is described in the sources of the Sages as an environment saturated with falsehood, deceit and idolatry, a reality that inspired the famous midrashic image in the Song of Songs: "As a rose among the thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters" [cite: 2, 3]. Rabbi Yitzchak expounded this verse as referring to Rebecca, noting that although her father, her brother and the people of her place were deceivers, this righteous woman managed to grow up entirely free of their corrupt influences [cite: 3]. It was this inner moral resilience that guided Abraham our Patriarch when he came to choose a bride for his son Isaac [cite: 2]. According to Midrash HaGadol, Abraham preferred to take a wife from his family in Haran even though they were idolaters, because he recognized in them a built-in moral potential of being "close to repentance" [cite: 2]. This quality helped them to free themselves from the husks (kelipot) of impurity of their place, and it found refined expression in Rebecca's autonomous personality [cite: 2].
Rebecca's chronology tells of a life path full of hardships and delays, which were transformed into instruments of spiritual elevation and prayer. Midrash HaGadol notes that Rebecca was only fourteen years old at the time of her marriage to Isaac, and that she lived one hundred and thirty-three years in all, like a group of biblical figures whose years were equal [cite: 1]. Twenty of her years she was barren, a long period intended, according to the accepted interpretation, to develop the shared power of prayer of her and Isaac [cite: 1, 4]. The Meta-Historical Role of Deborah the Nurse and Rebecca's Elevation in Holiness
Rebecca's journey from Haran to the land of Canaan is accompanied by spiritual intensity and cosmic symbols. The midrash describes that when Eliezer went to bring Rebecca, the Holy One, blessed be He, lit up the road for him with sparks and lightning, which points to the metaphysical importance of rescuing the rose from among the thorns [cite: 1]. On this journey Rebecca was accompanied by her nurse, Deborah [cite: 2]. Deborah's role was not only physical and practical but above all spiritual: to continue raising Rebecca in the levels of holiness, so that she would be worthy to join the holy seed of Isaac and to take her place in the building of the nation [cite: 2].
Deborah's influence as the one who carried on Rebecca's path is revealed on a deeper level at a later stage in the life of the family. According to Midrash Aggadah, when Isaac sent Jacob to Paddan Aram, Jacob remained with Laban and did not hasten to return to his father's house, despite Rebecca's promise to send for him [cite: 2]. Rebecca solved this difficulty by dispatching Deborah the nurse, who served as a kind of spiritual grandmother for Jacob, to bring him back from the bitter exile in Haran to the bosom of the family in the Land of Israel [cite: 2]. Deborah's death at Bethel and the great mourning for her reflect the closing of the circle of her national mission, which was intended to preserve the wholeness of the line [cite: 2]. Her passing also announced to Jacob the death of Rebecca herself, as the Sages hinted regarding the blessing with which God blessed Jacob on that occasion as a "blessing of mourners" for his mother [cite: 1].

An Activism of Kindness at the Well: The Anthropological and Metaphysical Test
Rebecca's conduct at the well is the first practical test of her Torah teaching, which is founded on an uncompromising activism of kindness [cite: 1, 7, 8]. Her meeting with Eliezer was not a chance event but a meticulous anthropological test intended to find the one who would carry on Abraham's path [cite: 1, 5]. The author of "Kli Yakar" explains that Rebecca's offer to water the camels as well ("I will draw for your camels also") goes beyond a norm of simple courtesy [cite: 8, 9]. He points to an inner linguistic link between the word "your camels" (gemalekha) and "acts of loving-kindness" (gemilut chesed), and explains that Rebecca's love of this quality was so natural and deep that she sought to apply the concept of kindness to everything called by this name, including the animals of the foreign servant [cite: 9].
According to the commentary of the Malbim, Eliezer examined Rebecca with highly critical eyes in order to rule out ulterior motives [cite: 10]. The words "And the man gazed at her, holding his peace" are explained by Eliezer's fear that Rebecca might be offering such exhausting and strenuous service in the expectation of receiving a monetary reward or a tip [cite: 10]. Had that been her motive, she would have been revealed as a base and greedy personality, which would have disqualified her from being Isaac's wife [cite: 10]. Eliezer's silence continued until the camels had finished drinking, in order to prove beyond any doubt that she was acting out of pure generosity of heart and complete altruism, without any self-interested motive [cite: 8, 10].
With Rebecca's entry into Sarah's tent, the spiritual repair (tikkun) she brought with her found expression [cite: 11]. The Sages teach that the three special blessings that had accompanied Sarah and departed with her death – a candle burning from Sabbath eve to Sabbath eve, a blessing found in the dough, and a cloud tied over the tent – returned and appeared immediately with Rebecca's arrival [cite: 11]. These three elements represent the principles of her teaching about the home:
A perpetually burning candle: symbolizes spiritual life, the inner dimension of the Torah and the light of the soul, which imbues the service of God in the home with vitality and enthusiasm [cite: 11, 12].
A blessing in the dough: represents the sanctity of matter and the flow of economic abundance through the fulfillment of the commandment of separating challah [cite: 11, 12].
A cloud tied over the tent: symbolizes the resting of the Divine Presence and the transcendent spiritual protection of the family unit from outside influences [cite: 11].

The Existential Crisis of the Pregnancy and the Cry "Why Am I Thus?"
Rebecca's pregnancy was accompanied by extraordinary suffering, described in the words "and the children struggled together within her" [cite: 6, 13]. The Sages interpreted the term "struggling" (retzitzah) as an expression of a prenatal theological and physical struggle: when Rebecca passed by the synagogues and study houses of Shem and Eber, Jacob would strain to come out; and when she passed by houses of idolatry, Esau would strain to come out [cite: 6]. This rupture prompted Rebecca's piercing cry: "If so, why am I thus?" (im ken lamah zeh anokhi) [cite: 6, 14]. Beyond these interpretations, the midrash reveals a further dramatic layer of the crisis. According to Midrash Tanchuma, Rebecca was in essence worthy of bringing forth the twelve tribes of Israel herself, with no need for a further generation in the line [cite: 1, 6]. This potential is hinted at in the wording of the divine answer she received: "Two nations are in your womb" (two), "and two peoples shall be separated from your bowels" (four), "and the one people shall be stronger than the other people" (six), and when this is multiplied by the two fetuses the number twelve is obtained [cite: 1, 6]. However, because of the intensity of the crisis and the complaint "Why am I thus?", the spiritual tribal potential was dispersed, and it passed to be realized in the next generation, through her son Jacob [cite: 1, 6]. Rebecca's active turning to inquire of the Lord presents an unprecedented religious model of direct dialogue with God, based on a demand to understand the meaning of suffering and of history [cite: 14].

The Hidden Communicative Rift: Holy Awe and the Concealment of the Prophecy
The relationship between Isaac and Rebecca is marked by conspicuous communication gaps and by a lack of sharing of critical prophetic information [cite: 17]. Rebecca kept in her heart the prophecy she had received, that "the elder shall serve the younger" [cite: 5], and did not share it with Isaac, which ultimately led to the need to act in roundabout ways at the time the blessings were given [cite: 17].
The Netziv of Volozhin, in his commentary "Ha'amek Davar," explains the root of this phenomenon against the background of their first meeting in the field [cite: 4, 17, 18]. When Rebecca saw Isaac for the first time, he was standing in prayer in the midst of a sublime spiritual revelation, and his appearance was awesome and frightening like an angel of God [cite: 4, 17, 18]. Her fear was so great that she fell from the camel and hurried to cover herself with a veil out of shame and reverence [cite: 4, 7, 17, 18].
The Netziv analyzes that from that moment on a permanent fear of her husband was fixed in Rebecca's heart [cite: 17, 18]. Unlike Sarah with Abraham or Rachel with Jacob, who were not afraid to rebuke their husbands or to argue with them, Rebecca never felt comfortable conducting an open and equal conversation with Isaac the righteous, who was "a perfect burnt offering" detached from the vanities of this world [cite: 17, 18]. This built-in gap prevented her from presenting to him the truth about Esau's character or telling him about the prophecy she had received [cite: 17].
The Netziv emphasizes that this dynamic was directed from above as part of individual providence [cite: 18]. Had Rebecca conducted an open dialogue with Isaac, the blessings would have been given to Jacob by way of direct discussion, but it was God's will that the blessings reach Jacob precisely through cunning and the wearing of Esau's garments, as part of a broader historical repair [cite: 17, 18].

The Transcendent Strategy of the Blessings and the Purity of the Seed for the Generations
The episode of Jacob's taking of the blessings under Rebecca's direction is perceived at first glance as an immoral act of trickery [cite: 5]. Nevertheless, Rebecca's Torah teaching sees in this action the practical application of a divine pedagogy that sometimes demands "cutting into living flesh" in order to save the future of the nation [cite: 19].
According to the author of "Sefat Emet," Isaac sought to separate the blessing of this world (matter and political power), which he wanted to give to Esau, from the spiritual blessing of Abraham, which he had intended for Jacob from the outset [cite: 20]. Isaac aspired to create a model of partnership in which Esau would serve as a material shell and physical shield for Jacob, who engages in Torah [cite: 20]. Rebecca, who knew well the power of hypocrisy and deceit from the house of Laban the Aramean, understood that such a separation would abandon Jacob and would allow Esau to subjugate and crush the world of the spirit [cite: 17, 19]. She knew that matter must be directly subordinate to the spirit, and that Jacob must also hold the instruments of this world in order to ensure the real physical existence of the people of Israel [cite: 19]. The act of impersonation was therefore in the category of "a necessity beyond reproach" [cite: 19].
Ensuring the Purity of the Tribes: The Meaning of "Hear, O Israel"
A profound theological perspective on Rebecca's action is revealed in a Midrash Aggadah on the verse "Now, my son, hearken (shema)" [cite: 1]. Rebecca turns to Jacob and says to him: "Just as all your days you listen to me, now too hearken" [cite: 1]. The midrash explains that Rebecca announced to Jacob in prophecy that he was destined to bring forth complete tribes in whom there would be no blemish at all, unlike Abraham, who begot Ishmael, and Isaac, who begot Esau [cite: 1].
Rebecca foresaw through the holy spirit the historic moment when Jacob would gather his sons before his death in order to reveal to them the end of days [cite: 1]. At that hour the Divine Presence departed from him, and Jacob was seized with fear that there might be some spiritual blemish in his sons preventing the revelation of the end [cite: 1]. At that dramatic moment, all his sons answered him with one voice: "Hear, O Israel" [cite: 1]. It was Rebecca's prophetic promise that gave Jacob the strength of spirit and the knowledge that "his bed was complete" and that his seed was entirely holy and pure, without any trace of spiritual dross [cite: 1].
The Teaching of the Garments and the Doctrine of the Clarification of the Sparks
The Hasidic thought of Chabad delves into the inner meaning of Jacob's wearing of Esau's goodly garments [cite: 21]. The move that Rebecca planned was intended to create an eternal connection with all the future parts of the people of Israel, and in particular with those who would outwardly look like Esau – Jews who wear everyday clothes and adopt the culture of the field [cite: 21].
Rebecca established the principle that outward appearance and dress do not determine the essence of a Jew; only his inner soul does [cite: 21]. Because Isaac blessed Jacob while he was clad in Esau's garments, he extended the blessings and the power of elevation also to those generations that would seemingly lose their outward identity [cite: 21].
This metaphysical depth is hinted at in the scent of the garments that Isaac smelled, of which it is said: "Do not read begadav (his garments) but bogdav (his traitors)" [cite: 21, 22]. Isaac smelled the fragrance of the souls of the greatest sinners and heretics who were destined to come forth from the people of Israel (such as Yosef Meshita and Yakum Ish Tzerorot), in whom, at the moment of truth of their lives, the Jewish spark awoke and they gave their lives for the sanctification of God's name [cite: 21]. Jacob, wearing Esau's garments, represents the ability of the people of Israel to descend into the depths of the husks (kelipot), to clarify the captive sparks of holiness there, and to turn even sin and betrayal into a scent of the Garden of Eden [cite: 21, 22].

Rebecca's Hidden Passing and the Burial by Night
The end of Rebecca our Matriarch is accompanied by a family tragedy that teaches about the existential complexity of her life as the nursing mother of two opposing nations [cite: 1]. According to the sources of the Sages, Rebecca's death was not announced publicly and her funeral was held in secret in the dead of night [cite: 1].
The midrashic reason for this night burial lies in the great fear of Esau [cite: 1]. The leaders of the generation feared that if Rebecca's bier were carried out by day, Esau the wicked would walk at the head of the funeral procession, and people would call out after her in horror: "Cursed be the breasts that suckled this wicked one" [cite: 1]. To prevent the disgrace of the righteous woman and the mingling of the wicked one's name in her funeral, they carried out her bier at night and concealed the fact of her burial in the Cave of Machpelah [cite: 1].
This concealment explains why the Torah does not explicitly describe her passing and the mourning for her, unlike Sarah and Rachel. This lack was made up only when Jacob returned from Paddan Aram, and God revealed Himself to him in order to give him the blessing of mourners for the death of his mother [cite: 1]. This painful reality is hinted at in the verse in Psalms: "and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out," which links Esau's wickedness with the dark shadow it cast over the passing and memory of his righteous mother [cite: 1].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A Leadership Synthesis and a Complete Torah Teaching
The analysis of the figure of Rebecca our Matriarch reveals a comprehensive Torah teaching that combines metaphysical theology with uncompromising leadership realism [cite: 5, 19]. Rebecca is revealed as the true architect of the line of Israel, who recognized the physical and spiritual needs of the nation even before they came into the world [cite: 19, 21].
Her work began with a self-education of separation from a corrupt environment [cite: 3], continued with an uncompromising activism of kindness at the well [cite: 7, 8], and reached its peak in leading complex historical moves intended to ensure the subordination of matter to spirit and the purity of the seed for the generations [cite: 19, 20, 21].
Her prophetic promise to Jacob that his sons would be whole, without any blemish [cite: 1], together with the creation of the spiritual instrument of "Esau's garments," which makes it possible to clarify the sparks of holiness even among those who drift away and betray [cite: 21], form the foundation and the coping-stones of Jewish existence throughout history. Rebecca our Matriarch leaves to the generations a model of leadership that is initiating, practical and courageous, shaping reality out of a vision of divine eternity [cite: 19].
